samples: This program reads a fixed file, `data/server.log`, where each line holds a timestamp, a severity level and a message. It prints how many error-level entries occurred in each date-and-hour bucket, earliest first, and hours with no errors are not listed. It needs read access to the filesystem and nothing else, but any malformed line or unrecognized level aborts the whole run with an error instead of being skipped (only blank lines are ignored), so it suits clean logs best. One caution: the grouping step omits a final collect or sum clause, a form the language reference doesn't show, so check that it compiles and behaves as intended before relying on it.

This program reads a fixed log file (data/server.log) in read-only mode, parses each non-blank line as a timestamp, a severity level and a message, and prints how many error-level entries occurred in each date-and-hour bucket, earliest first. It is strict: a single malformed line or unrecognized severity word aborts the whole run with an error instead of skipping that line, and hours with no errors are not listed. The path is hard-coded, so it is a sample tool rather than a reusable one, and one step that groups errors by hour has no explicit collect or sum, which the language reference doesn't show, so check that it compiles before relying on it.

This program reads the file `data/server.log`, where each line holds a timestamp, a severity level (DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR) and a message. It counts the ERROR entries per calendar hour and prints one line per hour, earliest first, so hours with no errors don't appear. It only reads files and prints, but the path is hardcoded, blank lines are skipped, and any malformed line or unknown level (including a line with no message) stops the whole run with an error instead of being skipped. One more point to check before relying on it: the grouping step in the counting function has no explicit "collect" or "sum" ending, which the cheat sheet always shows, so it may not compile as written.

This program reads a server log from a fixed file path (the data folder's server log), parses each non-blank line as a timestamp, a severity level and a message, and prints how many error-level entries occurred in each date-and-hour bucket, earliest first; hours with no errors don't appear. It needs only console and read-only filesystem access, but the path is hardcoded and a single malformed line or unknown level word (anything other than DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR) aborts the whole run with a failure instead of being skipped. One caveat: the step that groups errors by hour has no closing clause saying what to collect, which the cheat sheet's grouping examples all include, so it may not compile as written and is worth checking before you rely on it.

This program reads a fixed file, `data/server.log`, parses each non-blank line as a timestamp, a severity level (debug, info, warn or error) and a message, and prints how many error-level entries fall in each date-and-hour bucket, earliest first. It is a small, read-only demo rather than a configurable tool: the path is hardcoded, hours with no errors are not listed, and a single malformed line or unknown level aborts the whole run with a parse error instead of being skipped. One thing to check before relying on it is the grouping step, which uses a `group by` query with no `collect` or `sum` clause, a form the cheat sheet does not show, so it may not compile or behave as intended.
